statement: Let $L$ be a [unimodular lattice](c:unimodular-lattice) of finite rank and $c \in L$ a [characteristic element](c:characteristic-element). Then $c \cdot c \equiv \sigma(L) \pmod 8$, where $\sigma(L)$ is the [signature](c:signature) of $L$.

hypotheses.text: $L$ is a [unimodular lattice](c:unimodular-lattice) of finite rank: a free abelian group with an integral symmetric bilinear form of determinant $\pm 1$.
The element $c \in L$ is [characteristic](c:characteristic-element): $x \cdot x \equiv x \cdot c \pmod 2$ for every $x \in L$.

conclusion: The square $c \cdot c$ is congruent to the [signature](c:signature) $\sigma(L)$ modulo $8$.

proofs.name: Stabilize to a diagonal lattice
proofs.slogan: Add a rank-two summand to make the lattice odd and indefinite, diagonalize it, and read both sides modulo $8$.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, for even and odd $L$ and for rank $0$. The proof cites the classification of odd indefinite unimodular lattices.

roles.why: A [unimodular lattice](c:unimodular-lattice) stays unimodular after the stabilization, so the classification of indefinite lattices applies.
The [characteristic element](c:characteristic-element) $c$ extends to a characteristic element $c'$ with the same square, and $c'$ has odd coordinates.

steps.slogan: Add the summand $\langle 1 \rangle \oplus \langle -1 \rangle$ to make an odd indefinite lattice $L'$.
steps.detail: Let $L' = L \oplus \mathbb{Z}e \oplus \mathbb{Z}f$ with $e \cdot e = 1$, $f \cdot f = -1$ and $e \cdot f = 0$. The lattice $L'$ is [unimodular](c:unimodular-lattice), odd and indefinite, and $\sigma(L') = \sigma(L)$. The vector $c' = c + e + f$ is characteristic in $L'$, and $c' \cdot c' = c \cdot c + 1 - 1 = c \cdot c$.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize the odd indefinite lattice $L'$ over the integers.
steps.detail: An odd indefinite unimodular lattice is isomorphic to $\langle 1 \rangle^{p} \oplus \langle -1 \rangle^{q}$ (the classification of Serre and of Milnor and Husemoller, which rests on the Hasse-Minkowski theorem). Then $p - q = \sigma(L')$.

steps.slogan: Show that a characteristic element of the diagonal lattice has only odd coordinates.
steps.detail: Let $\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_{p+q}$ be the diagonal basis, with $\epsilon_i \cdot \epsilon_i = \pm 1$. Taking $x = \epsilon_i$ in $x \cdot x \equiv x \cdot w \pmod 2$ gives $w_i \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ for every characteristic $w = \sum w_i \epsilon_i$.

steps.slogan: Compute $c' \cdot c'$ modulo $8$ from the odd coordinates of $c'$.
steps.detail: Every odd integer squares to $1$ modulo $8$. So $c' \cdot c' = \sum_i \pm c_i'^2 \equiv p - q \pmod 8$, with $+$ for the $p$ positive basis vectors and $-$ for the $q$ negative ones. Hence $c \cdot c = c' \cdot c' \equiv p - q = \sigma(L) \pmod 8$.

concepts.c:unimodular-lattice: Unimodularity allows the stabilization and the classification of indefinite lattices.
concepts.c:characteristic-element: A characteristic element has odd coordinates in a diagonal basis.
concepts.c:signature: The signature $p - q$ is the count of positive minus negative basis vectors.

source.note: The stabilization argument with the diagonalization of odd indefinite unimodular lattices (Milnor and Husemoller, Symmetric Bilinear Forms, Chapter II; Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Chapter V).

statement:
Let $\mu$ be a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) and $
u_n$ complex measures that are [absolutely continuous](c:absolute-continuity) with respect to $\mu$. If $
u(A) = \lim_n 
u_n(A)$ exists for every measurable $A$, then the $
u_n$ are uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$, and $
u$ is a complex measure.

hypotheses.text: $\mu$ is a positive [finite measure](c:finite-measure) on a $\sigma$-algebra $\Sigma$.
Each $\nu_n$ is a complex measure on $\Sigma$ that is [absolutely continuous](c:absolute-continuity) with respect to $\mu$.
The limit $\nu(A) = \lim_n \nu_n(A)$ exists for every $A \in \Sigma$.

conclusion: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that $|\nu_n(A)| < \varepsilon$ for all $n$ whenever $\mu(A) < \delta$, and $\nu$ is countably additive.

proofs.name: Baire category on the measure algebra
proofs.slogan: Find a ball of sets on which the sequence is uniformly Cauchy by Baire category, then pass the bound to all small sets and to the limit.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for complex measures. Step 5 proves uniform absolute continuity and step 6 proves that $\nu$ is countably additive.

roles.why: Finiteness of $\mu$ makes $d(A,B) = \mu(A \triangle B)$ a finite metric and gives $\mu(B_N) \to 0$ for decreasing unions.
Absolute continuity makes each $\nu_n$ continuous for the metric $d$ and gives a $\delta$ for the first $k$ measures.
Convergence of $\nu_n(A)$ makes the sequence Cauchy for every set, and it defines $\nu$.

steps.slogan: Form the metric space of measurable sets modulo $\mu$-null sets.
steps.detail: Put $d(A,B) = \mu(A \triangle B)$ and identify sets at distance $0$. The map $A \mapsto \mathbf 1_A$ embeds this space isometrically as a closed subset of $L^1(\mu)$, so it is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space). Each $\nu_n$ is well defined and continuous on it, because $\nu_n$ is finite and [absolutely continuous](c:absolute-continuity) with respect to $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Cover the space by the closed sets $F_k$ where the sequence stays $\varepsilon$-Cauchy from index $k$.
steps.detail:
Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $F_k = \{A : |
u_n(A) - 
u_m(A)| \le \varepsilon 	ext{ for all } n, m \ge k\}$. Each $F_k$ is closed because each $
u_n$ is continuous. Since $
u_n(A)$ converges, it is Cauchy, so every set lies in some $F_k$.

steps.slogan: Select a ball $B(A_0, r)$ that lies inside one of the sets $F_k$.
steps.detail: The space is complete, so it is a [Baire space](c:baire-space), and it is the union of the countably many closed sets $F_k$. By the Baire category theorem one $F_k$ has an interior point: some ball $B(A_0, r)$ lies in $F_k$.

steps.slogan: Write each small set as a difference of two sets in the ball.
steps.detail:
Let $\mu(B) < r$. The sets $A_0 \cup B$ and $A_0 \setminus B$ are within $\mu(B) < r$ of $A_0$, so both lie in $F_k$, and $B = (A_0 \cup B) \setminus (A_0 \setminus B)$. Hence $
u_n(B) = 
u_n(A_0 \cup B) - 
u_n(A_0 \setminus B)$, and $|
u_n(B) - 
u_m(B)| \le 2\varepsilon$ for all $n, m \ge k$.

steps.slogan: Add the finitely many early measures to get one $\delta$ for all $n$.
steps.detail:
The finitely many measures $
u_1, \dots, 
u_k$ are [absolutely continuous](c:absolute-continuity), so some $\delta \le r$ gives $|
u_n(B)| < \varepsilon$ for $n \le k$ and $\mu(B) < \delta$. For $n > k$, $|
u_n(B)| \le |
u_k(B)| + 2\varepsilon < 3\varepsilon$. So $|
u_n(B)| < 3\varepsilon$ for all $n$ whenever $\mu(B) < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit $\nu$ is countably additive by the uniform bound.
steps.detail:
The limit $
u$ is finitely additive. Let $A =  igsqcup_j A_j$ and $B_N =  igcup_{j > N} A_j$. Because $\mu$ is finite, $\mu(B_N) 	o 0$, so the uniform bound gives $|
u(B_N)| \le \varepsilon$ for large $N$, and $|
u(A) - \sum_{j \le N} 
u(A_j)| = |
u(B_N)| \le \varepsilon$.

concepts.c:finite-measure: Finite measure gives a finite metric and makes tails of unions small.
concepts.c:absolute-continuity: It makes each $\nu_n$ continuous in the set metric and bounds small sets.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness of the set space is what Baire category needs.
concepts.c:baire-space: A complete metric space is a Baire space: one closed piece has interior.

source.note: The classical Baire category proof (Dunford and Schwartz, Linear Operators, Part I, Chapter III, section 7).

statement: For every prime $p \ge 5$, the [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) $\binom{2p-1}{p-1}$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $p^3$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is prime.
The prime satisfies $p \ge 5$.

proofs.name: Elementary symmetric sums of reciprocals
proofs.slogan: Write the binomial as a product, expand it in elementary symmetric sums of reciprocals, and show that two of those sums vanish modulo powers of $p$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The hypothesis $p \ge 5$ is needed: for $p = 3$ the coefficient $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ is not $1$ modulo $27$.

roles.why: Primality makes each $1/k$ with $k < p$ a $p$-adic integer and lets Fermat's little theorem fix the polynomial modulo $p$.
The bound $p \ge 5$ gives $p - 3 \ge 1$, so $p$ divides $s_{p-3}$ and the correction term vanishes.

steps.slogan: Write the binomial coefficient as a product of the fractions $(p+k)/k$.
steps.detail: $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} = \dfrac{(p+1)(p+2)\cdots(2p-1)}{(p-1)!} = \prod_{k=1}^{p-1} \left(1 + \dfrac{p}{k}\right)$. Each $1/k$ lies in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, the integers localized at $p$, because $p \nmid k$.

steps.slogan: Expand the product in the elementary symmetric sums $e_j$ of $1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1{p-1}$.
steps.detail: The product equals $1 + p\,e_1 + p^2 e_2 + p^3 R$ with $R \in \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, where $e_1 = \sum_k 1/k$ is the [harmonic number](c:harmonic-number) $H_{p-1}$ and $e_2 = \sum_{i<j} 1/(ij)$. It suffices to show $e_1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ and $e_2 \equiv 0 \pmod p$.

steps.slogan: Relate the sums $e_j$ to the coefficients of $f(x) = \prod_{k=1}^{p-1}(x - k)$.
steps.detail: Write $f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{p-1} (-1)^j s_j x^{p-1-j}$, so $s_j$ is the $j$-th elementary symmetric polynomial of $1, \dots, p-1$ and $s_{p-1} = (p-1)!$. Then $e_j = s_{p-1-j}/(p-1)!$, and $(p-1)!$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$. So the goal is $p^2 \mid s_{p-2}$ and $p \mid s_{p-3}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ divides $s_j$ for $1 \le j \le p-2$ by comparing $f$ with $x^{p-1} - 1$.
steps.detail: By Fermat's little theorem, $1, \dots, p-1$ are $p-1$ distinct roots of $x^{p-1} - 1$ in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$. Both $f$ and $x^{p-1} - 1$ are monic of degree $p-1$ with these roots, so they agree modulo $p$. Comparing coefficients gives $s_j \equiv 0 \pmod p$ for $1 \le j \le p-2$; in particular $p \mid s_{p-3}$ because $p \ge 5$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $f(p)$ in two ways to prove $p^2 \mid s_{p-2}$.
steps.detail: Since $p - k$ runs over $1, \dots, p-1$, $f(p) = (p-1)!$, so $\sum_{j=0}^{p-2} (-1)^j s_j p^{p-1-j} = 0$. Divide by $p$ and reduce modulo $p^2$: only $j = p-3$ and $j = p-2$ remain, giving $p\, s_{p-3} - s_{p-2} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$. Since $p \mid s_{p-3}$, we get $p^2 \mid s_{p-2}$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two divisibilities in the expansion to get the congruence modulo $p^3$.
steps.detail: Now $e_1 = s_{p-2}/(p-1)! \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ and $e_2 = s_{p-3}/(p-1)! \equiv 0 \pmod p$. So $p\,e_1$ and $p^2 e_2$ vanish modulo $p^3$, and the product is $1 \pmod{p^3}$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$. Hence the integer $\binom{2p-1}{p-1}$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The theorem is a congruence for this binomial coefficient.
concepts.c:harmonic-number: The first symmetric sum $e_1$ is the harmonic number $H_{p-1}$.

source.note: The classical proof by the polynomial $\prod (x - k)$, as in Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, section 7.8.

statement: Let $p, q \in \mathbb{C}[t]$ satisfy $\mathbb{C}[p, q] = \mathbb{C}[t]$, so that $t \mapsto (p(t), q(t))$ embeds the line in the [affine plane](c:affine-plane). Then some [polynomial automorphism](c:polynomial-automorphism) $\Phi$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$ satisfies $\Phi(t, 0) = (p(t), q(t))$ for all $t$.

hypotheses.text: The polynomials $p, q \in \mathbb{C}[t]$ satisfy $\mathbb{C}[p, q] = \mathbb{C}[t]$, so $t \mapsto (p(t), q(t))$ is a closed embedding of the [affine line](c:affine-line) in the plane.

conclusion: There is a polynomial automorphism $\Phi$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$ with $\Phi(t, 0) = (p(t), q(t))$ for every $t$.

proofs.name: Degree divisibility and elementary reduction
proofs.slogan: Show that one degree divides the other, strip the leading term by an elementary automorphism, and repeat until the embedding is a linear line.
proofs.scope: An outline: the divisibility of the degrees (the epimorphism theorem) rests on the cited work of Abhyankar and Moh, and the other steps are proved here. The ground field is $\mathbb{C}$.

roles.why: The equation $\mathbb{C}[p, q] = \mathbb{C}[t]$ is the input of the epimorphism theorem and stays true after every elementary automorphism.

steps.slogan: Note that elementary automorphisms keep the hypothesis $\mathbb{C}[p, q] = \mathbb{C}[t]$.
steps.detail: For a polynomial $h$, the maps $(x, y) \mapsto (x, y - h(x))$ and $(x, y) \mapsto (y, x)$ are [polynomial automorphisms](c:polynomial-automorphism) of the plane. They replace $(p, q)$ by $(p, q - h(p))$ or by $(q, p)$, and they leave the ring $\mathbb{C}[p, q]$ unchanged.

steps.slogan: Prove that one of the degrees $\deg p$ and $\deg q$ divides the other.
steps.detail: This is the epimorphism theorem of Abhyankar and Moh, proved independently by Suzuki. The cited proof studies the Puiseux expansion at infinity of the curve $t \mapsto (p(t), q(t))$ together with approximate roots, and shows that $t \in \mathbb{C}[p, q]$ forces the divisibility.

steps.slogan: Cancel the leading term of the polynomial of larger degree using the other polynomial.
steps.detail: Say $m = \deg p \le \deg q = n$. By step 2, $n = km$, so a constant $c$ gives $\deg(q - c\,p^k) < n$. The pair $(p, q - c\,p^k)$ still satisfies $\mathbb{C}[p, q - c\,p^k] = \mathbb{C}[t]$ by step 1. A swap handles the case $m > n$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the cancellation until one polynomial is constant and the other has degree one.
steps.detail: While both polynomials are nonconstant, step 3 strictly lowers $\deg p + \deg q$, so the process stops. It stops at a pair $(a, b)$ with $b$ constant; then $\mathbb{C}[a] = \mathbb{C}[t]$ forces $\deg a = 1$.

steps.slogan: Compose the elementary automorphisms and an affine map to move the embedding onto the line $(t, 0)$.
steps.detail: The steps give automorphisms $\Psi_1, \dots, \Psi_r$ with $\Psi_r \cdots \Psi_1(p(t), q(t)) = (at + b, c)$ and $a \ne 0$. An affine automorphism $\Lambda$ sends $(at + b, c)$ to $(t, 0)$. Then $\Phi = (\Lambda \Psi_r \cdots \Psi_1)^{-1}$ is a polynomial automorphism with $\Phi(t, 0) = (p(t), q(t))$.

concepts.c:affine-plane: The embedded line lives in the affine plane that the automorphism acts on.
concepts.c:polynomial-automorphism: Elementary and affine automorphisms reduce the embedding to a line.
concepts.c:affine-line: The line $\mathbb{C}$ with coordinate $t$ is the embedded curve.

source.ref: S. S. Abhyankar and T. T. Moh, Embeddings of the line in the plane, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 276 (1975), 148-166
source.note: Step 2 is the epimorphism theorem of this paper; M. Suzuki proved it independently in J. Math. Soc. Japan 26 (1974), 241-257. Steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 are the elementary reduction.

statement: Let $BP$ be the [Brown-Peterson spectrum](c:brown-peterson-spectrum) at a prime $p$. Then $BP_*BP = BP_*[t_1, t_2, \dots]$ with $|t_i| = 2(p^i - 1)$, and $(BP_*, BP_*BP)$ is a [Hopf algebroid](c:hopf-algebroid) that represents strict isomorphisms of $p$-typical [formal group laws](c:formal-group-law).

hypotheses.text: $BP$ is the [Brown-Peterson spectrum](c:brown-peterson-spectrum) at the prime $p$.
The number $p$ is prime.

conclusion: The ring $BP_*BP$ is the polynomial ring $BP_*[t_1, t_2, \dots]$, and $(BP_*, BP_*BP)$ is a Hopf algebroid representing strict isomorphisms of $p$-typical formal group laws.

proofs.name: Strict isomorphisms of p-typical laws
proofs.slogan: Split $BP$ off complex cobordism, identify $BP_*BP$ with strict isomorphisms of $p$-typical laws, and coordinatize them by the $t_i$.
proofs.scope: An outline: each step follows the cited books, which prove the full statement. The complex cobordism input is Quillen's theorem and the structure of $MU_*MU$.

roles.why: $BP$ is a retract of $MU_{(p)}$, so its homology theory inherits the Hopf algebroid structure of $MU_*MU$.
The prime $p$ lets Cartier's theorem make every formal group law over a $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebra strictly isomorphic to a $p$-typical one.

steps.slogan: Start from the structure $MU_*MU = MU_*[b_1, b_2, \dots]$ of complex cobordism.
steps.detail: Quillen's theorem gives $MU_* \cong L$, the Lazard ring of the universal formal group law. Adams shows that $MU_*MU$ represents strict isomorphisms $x \mapsto x + \sum b_i x^{i+1}$ between formal group laws, so $(MU_*, MU_*MU)$ is a Hopf algebroid.

steps.slogan: Split $BP$ off $MU_{(p)}$ by Quillen's idempotent.
steps.detail: Cartier's theorem makes each formal group law over a $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebra strictly isomorphic to a unique [p-typical law](c:p-typical-formal-group-law). This gives an idempotent $\varepsilon$ of $MU_{(p)}$ whose image is $BP$, and $BP_* = \mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[v_1, v_2, \dots]$ is the ring of the universal $p$-typical law.

steps.slogan: Identify $BP_*BP$ with the ring of strict isomorphisms between two $p$-typical laws.
steps.detail: Since $BP$ is a retract of $MU_{(p)}$, $BP \wedge BP$ is a retract of $MU \wedge MU$ after localization. So $BP_*BP$ is the quotient of $MU_*MU_{(p)}$ that classifies a strict isomorphism between two $p$-typical laws.

steps.slogan: Write every strict isomorphism of $p$-typical laws as $\sum^F t_i x^{p^i}$ with $t_0 = 1$.
steps.detail: A strict isomorphism $f$ from a $p$-typical law $F$ to a $p$-typical law $G$ has the form $f^{-1}(x) = \sum^F_{i \ge 0} t_i x^{p^i}$ with $t_0 = 1$, and the $t_i$ are free coordinates. Hence $BP_*BP = BP_*[t_1, t_2, \dots]$, and $|t_i| = 2(p^i - 1)$ by degree count.

steps.slogan: Read the Hopf algebroid maps off composition and inversion of strict isomorphisms.
steps.detail: The two units send $BP_*$ to the source and target laws, the coproduct is composition of strict isomorphisms, and the conjugation is inversion. The Hopf algebroid axioms hold because they hold for the groupoid of strict isomorphisms, and $BP_*BP$ is free, hence flat, over $BP_*$.

concepts.c:brown-peterson-spectrum: $BP$ is the spectrum split off complex cobordism at $p$.
concepts.c:hopf-algebroid: The pair of rings with its units and coproduct is the Hopf algebroid in question.
concepts.c:p-typical-formal-group-law: $p$-typical laws are the objects that $BP_*$ classifies.
concepts.c:formal-group-law: Strict isomorphisms of formal group laws are what $BP_*BP$ represents.

source.ref: J. F. Adams, Stable Homotopy and Generalised Homology, University of Chicago Press, 1974, Part II; D. C. Ravenel, Complex Cobordism and Stable Homotopy Groups of Spheres, Academic Press, 1986 (second edition AMS Chelsea, 2004), Chapter 4 and Appendix 2
source.note: Adams treats MU_*MU and Quillen's theorem; Ravenel proves the structure of BP_*BP and the representing property.

statement: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) with distribution functions $F_1, \dots, F_n$. The joint distribution function of the [order statistics](c:order-statistic) $X_{(j_1)}, \dots, X_{(j_k)}$ at points $x_1 < \dots < x_k$ is a sum of [permanents](c:permanent) of $n \times n$ matrices built from the differences $F_r(x_l) - F_r(x_{l-1})$, divided by factorials.

hypotheses.text: $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables), not necessarily identically distributed.
The points satisfy $x_1 < \dots < x_k$ and the ranks satisfy $1 \le j_1 < \dots < j_k \le n$.

conclusion: With $x_0 = -\infty$, $x_{k+1} = \infty$ and $p_{r,l} = F_r(x_l) - F_r(x_{l-1})$, the probability $P(X_{(j_l)} \le x_l \text{ for } l = 1, \dots, k)$ equals $\sum_m \operatorname{Perm}(A_m) / (m_1! \cdots m_{k+1}!)$ over all $m \in \mathbb{N}^{k+1}$ with $m_1 + \dots + m_{k+1} = n$ and $m_1 + \dots + m_l \ge j_l$ for $l \le k$, where row $r$ of the $n \times n$ matrix $A_m$ lists $p_{r,l}$ exactly $m_l$ times for $l = 1, \dots, k+1$.

proofs.name: Counting by cells
proofs.slogan: Count how many variables fall in each interval, and write the probability of each count vector as a permanent over factorials.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any distribution functions. Ties among the $X_r$ do not matter, because every event below is defined by counts.

roles.why: Independence turns the probability of an assignment of variables to intervals into a product.
Increasing points cut the line into disjoint intervals, and increasing ranks give consistent count constraints.

steps.slogan: Rewrite each rank event as a count event.
steps.detail: Let $N(x) = \#\{r : X_r \le x\}$. Then $X_{(j)} \le x$ holds exactly when $N(x) \ge j$, with ties included, because the $j$-th smallest value is at most $x$ if and only if at least $j$ values are. So the [order statistic](c:order-statistic) event is $\{N(x_l) \ge j_l \text{ for all } l\}$.

steps.slogan: Split the event by the exact number $m_l$ of variables in each interval.
steps.detail: Put $I_l = (x_{l-1}, x_l]$ and $m_l = \#\{r : X_r \in I_l\}$. Then $\sum_l m_l = n$ and $N(x_l) = m_1 + \dots + m_l$. The event is the disjoint union, over the vectors $m$ with $m_1 + \dots + m_l \ge j_l$, of the events $\{$exactly $m_l$ variables lie in $I_l$ for all $l\}$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the assignments of variables to intervals, using independence.
steps.detail: An assignment $\varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to \{1, \dots, k+1\}$ with $|\varphi^{-1}(l)| = m_l$ has probability $\prod_r p_{r,\varphi(r)}$, because the $X_r$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables). The event with counts $m$ is the disjoint union of these assignment events, so its probability is $\sum_\varphi \prod_r p_{r,\varphi(r)}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the sum over assignments equals $\operatorname{Perm}(A_m) / (m_1! \cdots m_{k+1}!)$.
steps.detail: The [permanent](c:permanent) is $\operatorname{Perm}(A_m) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_r (A_m)_{r,\sigma(r)}$. Let $\beta(s)$ be the block of column $s$, so $(A_m)_{r,s} = p_{r,\beta(s)}$. Each assignment $\varphi$ equals $\beta \circ \sigma$ for exactly $\prod_l m_l!$ permutations $\sigma$, hence $\operatorname{Perm}(A_m) = \prod_l m_l! \sum_\varphi \prod_r p_{r,\varphi(r)}$.

steps.slogan: Add the probabilities of the disjoint count events over all admissible vectors $m$.
steps.detail: By step 2, the target probability is the sum over admissible $m$ of the probability of the count event. By steps 3 and 4, that probability is $\operatorname{Perm}(A_m) / (m_1! \cdots m_{k+1}!)$. This is the stated formula.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence makes the probability of an assignment a product of cell probabilities.
concepts.c:order-statistic: The rank events of the order statistics become count events.
concepts.c:permanent: The permanent counts assignments with weights, up to the factorial factor.

source.note: The counting proof of R. B. Bapat and M. I. Beg, Order statistics for nonidentically distributed variables and permanents, Sankhya Series A 51 (1989), 79-93.

statement: A topological space is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) if and only if it is [regular](c:regular-space), [T0](c:t0-space) and has a [σ-discrete base](c:sigma-discrete-base).

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a topological space.

conclusion: The space $X$ is metrizable if and only if it is regular and $T_0$ and has a base that is a countable union of discrete families.

proofs.name: Stone's theorem and the Nagata-Smirnov theorem
proofs.slogan: Get a $\sigma$-discrete base of a metric space from Stone's theorem, and get metrizability back from the Nagata-Smirnov theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole equivalence. A regular $T_0$ space is Hausdorff, so the Nagata-Smirnov theorem applies to it.

roles.why: Each direction starts from an arbitrary topological space and uses only the stated properties.

steps.slogan: Show that a metrizable space is regular and $T_0$.
steps.detail: A metric space is Hausdorff, hence $T_0$. For a closed set $C$ and a point $x \notin C$, put $r = d(x, C)/2 > 0$. The open sets $B(x, r)$ and $\{y : d(y, C) < r\}$ are disjoint, so the space is [regular](c:regular-space).

steps.slogan: Refine the cover of a metric space by $1/n$-balls to a $\sigma$-discrete open cover.
steps.detail: Let $(X, d)$ be a [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) space. For each $n$, Stone's theorem (every open cover of a metric space has a $\sigma$-discrete open refinement) gives an open refinement $\mathcal{V}_n$ of the cover by balls of radius $1/n$, and $\mathcal{V}_n$ is a countable union of discrete families. Each member of $\mathcal{V}_n$ has diameter at most $2/n$.

steps.slogan: Collect the refinements over all $n$ into one $\sigma$-discrete base.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{B} = \bigcup_n \mathcal{V}_n$. A countable union of $\sigma$-discrete families is $\sigma$-discrete. If $x \in U$ with $U$ open, choose $n$ with $B(x, 3/n) \subseteq U$ and $V \in \mathcal{V}_n$ with $x \in V$; then $V \subseteq B(x, 3/n) \subseteq U$, so $\mathcal{B}$ is a [σ-discrete base](c:sigma-discrete-base).

steps.slogan: Turn a $\sigma$-discrete base into a $\sigma$-locally finite base.
steps.detail: A discrete family is a [locally finite family](c:locally-finite-family): each point has a neighborhood that meets at most one member. So a union of countably many discrete families is a union of countably many locally finite families.

steps.slogan: Conclude metrizability from the Nagata-Smirnov theorem.
steps.detail: The Nagata-Smirnov theorem says that a regular Hausdorff space with a $\sigma$-locally finite base is metrizable. A regular $T_0$ space is Hausdorff, and step 4 gives the base, so the space is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space).

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 show that a metrizable space is regular, $T_0$ and has a $\sigma$-discrete base. Steps 4 and 5 show the converse. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:metrizable-space: Metrizability is the property that the criterion characterizes.
concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity separates points from closed sets, in both directions of the proof.
concepts.c:t0-space: With regularity, the $T_0$ property gives the Hausdorff property.
concepts.c:sigma-discrete-base: A $\sigma$-discrete base is the structure that metric spaces always have.
concepts.c:locally-finite-family: Discrete families are locally finite, which links Bing's condition to Nagata-Smirnov.

source.note: R. H. Bing, Metrization of topological spaces, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 3 (1951), 175-186; the sufficiency here reduces to the Nagata-Smirnov theorem (Engelking, General Topology, section 4.4).

statement: Let $X$ be a set with $n \ge 1$ elements and $\mathcal{F}$ a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of $n$ distinct subsets of $X$. Then some $x \in X$ has the property that the sets $F \setminus \{x\}$ with $F \in \mathcal{F}$ are still pairwise distinct.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ has $n \ge 1$ elements.
$\mathcal{F}$ is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of $n$ distinct subsets of $X$.

conclusion: Some $x \in X$ makes the $n$ sets $F \setminus \{x\}$ pairwise distinct.

proofs.name: A graph with n edges and a cycle
proofs.slogan: Assume that every element fails, build a graph with $n$ vertices and $n$ edges, and find a cycle that contradicts the distinct labels.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $n = 1$, where the assumption of step 1 is already impossible. The graph is simple, so a cycle has at least three edges.

roles.why: Each element of $X$ gives one edge, so the graph has $n$ edges.
The $n$ distinct sets are the vertices, and distinctness makes each pair of sets differ in a definite way.

steps.slogan: Assume that deleting any element makes two sets of $\mathcal{F}$ equal.
steps.detail: Suppose that for every $x \in X$ there are $A_x \ne B_x$ in $\mathcal{F}$ with $A_x \setminus \{x\} = B_x \setminus \{x\}$. Because $A_x \ne B_x$, this says $A_x \triangle B_x = \{x\}$.

steps.slogan: Build a graph on $\mathcal{F}$ with one edge $A_x B_x$ for each $x$.
steps.detail: The [graph](c:graph) $G$ has the $n$ sets as vertices and the edges $\{A_x, B_x\}$ labeled by $x \in X$. An edge $\{A, B\}$ determines its label by $A \triangle B = \{x\}$, so different $x$ give different edges. Hence $G$ is a simple graph with $n$ vertices and $n$ edges.

steps.slogan: Find a cycle in $G$, because a forest on $n$ vertices has at most $n - 1$ edges.
steps.detail: Each component of a forest is a [tree](c:tree), and a tree on $v$ vertices has $v - 1$ edges, so a forest on $n$ vertices has at most $n - 1$ edges. Therefore $G$ contains a cycle $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_m, A_1$ with $m \ge 3$, and its edges carry $m$ distinct labels $x_1, \dots, x_m$.

steps.slogan: Add the symmetric differences of consecutive sets around the cycle.
steps.detail: Each $A_i$ occurs twice in $(A_1 \triangle A_2) \triangle (A_2 \triangle A_3) \triangle \cdots \triangle (A_m \triangle A_1)$, so the sum is $\emptyset$. The same sum equals $\{x_1\} \triangle \cdots \triangle \{x_m\} = \{x_1, \dots, x_m\}$, because the labels are distinct.

steps.slogan: Compare the two values of the sum to obtain a contradiction.
steps.detail: The set $\{x_1, \dots, x_m\}$ is nonempty and also equals $\emptyset$. This contradiction shows that the assumption of step 1 is false, so some $x$ keeps all $n$ sets distinct.

concepts.c:family-of-sets: The $n$ distinct sets of the family are the vertices of the graph.
concepts.c:graph: The pairs of sets that differ in one element form the edges of the graph.
concepts.c:tree: Trees have one edge fewer than vertices, which forces a cycle in $G$.

source.note: The standard graph argument for J. A. Bondy, Induced subsets, Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series B 12 (1972), 201-202.

statement: For charged particles in a doubly connected region, a shift of the enclosed magnetic flux $\Phi$ by an integer multiple of $\Phi_0 = hc/e$ is undone by a [gauge transformation](c:gauge-transformation). So the spectrum and all gauge-invariant expectation values are periodic in $\Phi$ with period $\Phi_0$.

hypotheses.text: The particles move in a region $\Omega$ that is an [annulus](c:annulus), or any region whose loops wind around one hole with an integer winding number.

The [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) is $H(A) = \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{1}{2m}\big(\mathbf{p}_j - \tfrac{e}{c}A(\mathbf{r}_j)\big)^2 + V(\mathbf{r}_1, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N)$ with $V$ a single-valued function of the positions, and the boundary conditions are preserved by phase factors.
The vector potential $A$ is curl-free in $\Omega$ and has circulation $\Phi$ around the hole.

conclusion: For every integer $n$ there is a unitary $U_n$, a product of single-valued phases $e^{i n \theta_j}$ and $e^{i e g(\mathbf{r}_j)/\hbar c}$, with $H(A') = U_n H(A) U_n^{-1}$ for every curl-free $A'$ of circulation $\Phi + n\Phi_0$.

proofs.name: Single-valued gauge phase
proofs.slogan: Compare the two vector potentials, absorb their difference into a single-valued phase, and conjugate the Hamiltonian by that phase.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any number $N$ of particles and any single-valued potential $V$. Physical properties mean the spectrum and expectation values of gauge-invariant observables.

roles.why: On a region with one hole, a curl-free field is fixed by its circulation up to a gradient of a single-valued function.
The circulations $\Phi$ and $\Phi + n\Phi_0$ make the phase $e^{i e \chi / \hbar c}$ single valued.
Minimal coupling and a position-only potential let the phase cancel in the kinetic term and commute with $V$.

steps.slogan: Compare two curl-free potentials whose circulations differ by $n\Phi_0$.
steps.detail:
Let $	heta$ be the angle around the hole. The field $A' - A -  rac{n\Phi_0}{2\pi}
abla	heta$ is curl-free with zero circulation, so by the Poincaré lemma and path independence it equals $
abla g$ for a single-valued function $g$. Hence $A' = A + 
abla\chi$ with $\chi =  rac{n\Phi_0}{2\pi}	heta + g$.

steps.slogan: Show that the phase $e^{ie\chi/\hbar c}$ is single valued.
steps.detail: Since $\Phi_0 = 2\pi\hbar c/e$, $e\chi/\hbar c = n\theta + e g/\hbar c$. One turn around the hole changes $\theta$ by $2\pi$, so $e^{in\theta}$ returns to its value, and $g$ is single valued. So $U = \prod_j e^{ie\chi(\mathbf{r}_j)/\hbar c}$ is a well-defined unitary operator.

steps.slogan: Conjugate the kinetic term by $U$ and see that $\nabla\chi$ cancels.
steps.detail:
For one particle, $ ig(\mathbf{p} -  rac{e}{c}(A + 
abla\chi) ig) ig(e^{ie\chi/\hbar c}\psi ig) = e^{ie\chi/\hbar c} ig(\mathbf{p} -  rac{e}{c}A ig)\psi$, because $\mathbf{p} = -i\hbar
abla$ acting on the phase gives $+ rac{e}{c}
abla\chi$. The potential $V$ depends on positions only, so it commutes with $U$. Hence $H(A') = U H(A) U^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the spectrum and the gauge-invariant expectation values between the two fluxes.
steps.detail: The [unitary equivalence](c:unitary-equivalence) $H(A') = UH(A)U^{-1}$ preserves the spectrum and maps an eigenfunction $\psi$ to $U\psi$. A gauge-invariant observable $O$ becomes $O' = UOU^{-1}$, so $\langle U\psi, O' U\psi\rangle = \langle\psi, O\psi\rangle$. So every physical property repeats when $\Phi$ changes by $\Phi_0$.

concepts.c:gauge-transformation: The shift of flux by $n\Phi_0$ is exactly a gauge transformation.
concepts.c:annulus: The hole makes loops wind, so circulation is the only invariant of the potential.
concepts.c:hamiltonian: The Hamiltonian is the operator that the gauge phase conjugates.
concepts.c:unitary-equivalence: Unitary equivalence preserves the spectrum and the gauge-invariant expectation values.

source.note: The gauge-transformation argument of N. Byers and C. N. Yang, Theoretical considerations concerning quantized magnetic flux in superconducting cylinders, Physical Review Letters 7 (1961), 46-49.

statement: For a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$ and $r > 0$, the [Nevanlinna characteristic](c:nevanlinna-characteristic) $T(r, f)$ equals the [circle average](c:circle-average) over $|a| = 1$ of $N(r, a) + \log|c_a|$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on $\mathbb{C}$.
The radius $r$ is positive.

conclusion: $T(r, f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \big(N(r, e^{i\theta}) + \log|c_{e^{i\theta}}|\big)\,d\theta$, where $N(r, a)$ is the [counting function](c:counting-function) of the $a$-points of $f$ and $c_a$ is the first nonzero Laurent coefficient of $f - a$ at $0$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any real radius $R \ne 0$, while this statement takes $r > 0$. It writes the result as a sum of two circle averages, which equals the average of the sum because both terms are circle integrable.

proofs.name: Jensen's formula and a double circle average
proofs.slogan: Write the proximity term as a double circle average, apply Jensen's formula for each value $a$, and split the average.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $r > 0$. The characteristic is taken at the value $\infty$, so $T(r, f) = m(r, f) + N(r, f)$.

roles.why: Meromorphy makes the circle averages exist and lets Jensen's formula apply to $f - a$ for every $a$.
A positive radius gives a genuine circle on which the averages and Jensen's formula are taken.

steps.slogan: Split the characteristic into its proximity part and its counting part at the value $\infty$.
steps.detail: By definition, $T(r, f) = m(r, f) + N(r, f)$, where $m(r, f) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \log^+|f(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta$ is the proximity function and $N(r, f)$ is the [counting function](c:counting-function) of the poles of $f$.

steps.slogan: Write the proximity term as an average over $a$ of the average of $\log|f - a|$.
steps.detail: For each $w \in \mathbb{C}$, the [circle average](c:circle-average) of $\log|w - a|$ over $|a| = 1$ equals $\log^+|w|$, by Jensen's formula for the function $z \mapsto z - w$. Put $w = f(re^{i\theta})$, average over $\theta$ and exchange the two integrals by Fubini's theorem to get $m(r, f) = \operatorname{avg}_{|a| = 1}\operatorname{avg}_\theta \log|f(re^{i\theta}) - a|$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite each inner average by Jensen's formula for the function $f - a$.
steps.detail: For every $a$, the zeros of $f - a$ are the $a$-points of $f$ and its poles are the poles of $f$. Jensen's formula gives $\operatorname{avg}_\theta \log|f(re^{i\theta}) - a| + N(r, f) = N(r, a) + \log|c_a|$.

steps.slogan: Add the constant $N(r, f)$ inside the average and split it into two circle averages.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $T(r, f) = \operatorname{avg}_{|a|=1}\big(N(r, a) + \log|c_a|\big)$, because $N(r, f)$ does not depend on $a$. Both $a \mapsto N(r, a)$ and $a \mapsto \log|c_a|$ are circle integrable, so the average also splits into the two averages of the [Nevanlinna characteristic](c:nevanlinna-characteristic) formula.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: Meromorphy is the hypothesis that makes Jensen's formula and the averages work.
concepts.c:nevanlinna-characteristic: The characteristic $T(r, f)$ is the quantity that the formula computes.
concepts.c:counting-function: The counting functions $N(r, a)$ of the $a$-points appear on the right side.
concepts.c:circle-average: The proof turns the proximity term into iterated circle averages.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the proximity function as an iterated circle average (circleAverage_circleAverage_eq_proximity_top), applies a Jensen-type identity for each a (logCounting_add_log_trailingCoeff_eq_circleAverage_add_logCounting_top), and splits the average with circleAverage_add.

statement: Let $T$ be a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) with $T \vdash \forall \bar y\, \exists x\, \varphi(\bar y, x)$. Let $T'$ add a new function symbol $f$ and the axiom $\forall \bar y\, \varphi(\bar y, f(\bar y))$. Then $T'$ is a [conservative extension](c:conservative-extension) of $T$: every sentence of the old language provable in $T'$ is provable in $T$.

hypotheses.text: $T$ is a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) in a language $L$.
For an $L$-formula $\varphi(\bar y, x)$, the theory proves $\forall \bar y\, \exists x\, \varphi(\bar y, x)$.
$f$ is a new function symbol (a constant when $\bar y$ is empty), and $T' = T \cup \{\forall \bar y\, \varphi(\bar y, f(\bar y))\}$ in the language $L \cup \{f\}$.

conclusion: Every $L$-sentence provable from $T'$ is provable from $T$.

proofs.name: Expand each model by a choice function
proofs.slogan: Expand a model of $T$ that falsifies a sentence by a choice function for $\varphi$, then use completeness to move between proofs and models.
proofs.scope: The case of one new function symbol; a new constant is the case of no variables $\bar y$, and an [extension by definitions](c:extension-by-definitions) is the case where the witness $x$ is unique. The converse, that $T$ proves what $T'$ proves for the old language, is not needed, because $T \subseteq T'$.

roles.why: The axioms of $T$ hold in the model $M$ and still hold after the expansion, because $L$-formulas ignore $f$.
The provable sentence $\forall \bar y\, \exists x\, \varphi$ holds in $M$, so every tuple has a witness.
The new axiom says that $f$ picks a witness, which is exactly what the expansion provides.

steps.slogan: Assume that an $L$-sentence $\psi$ is not provable from $T$, and take a model of $T$ falsifying it.
steps.detail:
We prove the contrapositive: if $T 
vdash \psi$ then $T' 
vdash \psi$. By the completeness theorem, $T 
vdash \psi$ gives a [model](c:model-type) $M$ of $T \cup \{
eg\psi\}$.

steps.slogan: Note that every tuple of $M$ has a witness for $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Since $M \models T$ and $T \vdash \forall \bar y\, \exists x\, \varphi$, soundness gives $M \models \forall \bar y\, \exists x\, \varphi$. So for each tuple $\bar b \in M^n$ the set $W(\bar b) = \{a \in M : M \models \varphi(\bar b, a)\}$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Choose a witness $f^M(\bar b) \in W(\bar b)$ for every tuple $\bar b$.
steps.detail: The axiom of choice gives a function $f^M \colon M^n \to M$ with $f^M(\bar b) \in W(\bar b)$ for all $\bar b$. When $n = 0$, this is the choice of one element of $W$.

steps.slogan: Expand $M$ to an $(L \cup \{f\})$-structure $M^*$ that interprets $f$ as $f^M$.
steps.detail: The structure $M^*$ has the same universe and the same $L$-structure as $M$, so it satisfies every axiom of $T$. The new axiom holds in $M^*$ by the choice of $f^M$. Hence $M^* \models T'$.

steps.slogan: Transfer $\neg\psi$ to $M^*$ and conclude that $T'$ does not prove $\psi$.
steps.detail: The sentence $\psi$ is an $L$-sentence, so it has the same truth value in $M^*$ as in $M$, and $M^* \models \neg\psi$. A model of $T'$ that falsifies $\psi$ shows $T' \nvdash \psi$, by soundness. So every $L$-sentence provable from $T'$ is provable from $T$.

concepts.c:first-order-theory: The theory $T$ and its extension $T'$ are the objects compared.
concepts.c:conservative-extension: Conservativity is the property to prove: no new old-language theorems.
concepts.c:extension-by-definitions: Extension by definitions is the member of the family with a unique witness.
concepts.c:model-type: A model of $T$ falsifying $\psi$ is expanded to a model of $T'$.

source.note: The semantic proof through the completeness theorem, as in the treatment of conservative extensions in Shoenfield, Mathematical Logic, Chapter 4.

statement: If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) and $X_1 + X_2$ has a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution), then $X_1$ and $X_2$ are normal. A point mass counts as a degenerate normal law.

hypotheses.text: $X_1$ and $X_2$ are [independent random variables](c:independent-random-variables) with real values.
The sum $X_1 + X_2$ has a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) $N(m, s^2)$.

conclusion: Each of $X_1$ and $X_2$ has a normal distribution, possibly with variance $0$.

proofs.name: Entire characteristic functions without zeros
proofs.slogan: Show that the characteristic functions are entire of order at most two and have no zeros, so each is the exponential of a quadratic polynomial.
proofs.scope: The main case is $s > 0$. If $s = 0$, then $\varphi_1\varphi_2 = e^{imt}$ with $|\varphi_i| \le 1$ gives $|\varphi_1| = 1$, so $X_1$ and $X_2$ are constants.

roles.why: Independence makes the characteristic function of the sum the product $\varphi_1\varphi_2$, and gives the tail bound by conditioning.
The Gaussian tails and the explicit nonvanishing characteristic function of the sum control $X_1$ and $X_2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tails of $X_1$ and $X_2$ by the Gaussian tails of the sum.
steps.detail: Choose $a$ with $P(X_2 \ge -a) \ge \tfrac12$ and $P(X_2 \le a) \ge \tfrac12$. Independence gives $P(X_1 > t) \le 2P(X_1 + X_2 > t - a)$ and $P(X_1 < -t) \le 2P(X_1 + X_2 < -t + a)$. So $P(|X_1| > t) \le 4e^{-(t - |a| - |m|)^2/(2s^2)}$ for large $t$, and $X_2$ satisfies the same bound.

steps.slogan: Extend the characteristic function of each $X_i$ to an entire function of order at most two.
steps.detail: The tail bound gives $E\,e^{\varepsilon X_i^2} < \infty$ for small $\varepsilon > 0$. So $\varphi_i(z) = E\,e^{izX_i}$ converges for every complex $z$ and is an [entire function](c:entire-function). Since $|z||x| \le \varepsilon x^2 + |z|^2/(4\varepsilon)$, $|\varphi_i(z)| \le C e^{|z|^2/(4\varepsilon)}$.

steps.slogan: Extend the product identity $\varphi_1\varphi_2 = \varphi$ to the whole complex plane.
steps.detail: On the real line, $\varphi_1(t)\varphi_2(t) = e^{imt - s^2t^2/2}$, by independence and the normal law. Both sides are entire, so the identity theorem gives $\varphi_1(z)\varphi_2(z) = e^{imz - s^2z^2/2}$ for all $z \in \mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi_1$ has no zero and write $\varphi_1 = e^{g}$ with $g$ entire.
steps.detail: The product $\varphi_1\varphi_2$ never vanishes, so neither factor vanishes. A zero-free entire function is $e^{g}$ for an entire $g$, because the plane is simply connected. Then $\operatorname{Re} g(z) = \log|\varphi_1(z)| \le \log C + |z|^2/(4\varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ is a polynomial of degree at most two.
steps.detail: The Borel-Caratheodory inequality turns the bound on $\operatorname{Re} g$ into $\max_{|z| = r}|g| = O(r^2)$. Cauchy's estimates then force every Taylor coefficient of $g$ above degree two to vanish.

steps.slogan: Identify $e^{g}$ as the characteristic function of a normal law.
steps.detail: Write $g(z) = c_1 z + c_2 z^2$ with $g(0) = 0$. The identity $\varphi_1(-t) = \overline{\varphi_1(t)}$ gives $c_1 = i\mu$ with $\mu$ real and $c_2$ real, and $|\varphi_1(t)| \le 1$ gives $c_2 = -\sigma^2/2 \le 0$. Then $\varphi_1(t) = e^{i\mu t - \sigma^2t^2/2}$, so $X_1 \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ by uniqueness of characteristic functions, and the same holds for $X_2$.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence gives the product of characteristic functions and the tail bound.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Normality of the sum fixes the product $\varphi_1\varphi_2$ and its tails.
concepts.c:entire-function: Entire characteristic functions allow zero-free factorization and growth estimates.

source.note: The standard characteristic-function proof of H. Cramér, Über eine Eigenschaft der normalen Verteilungsfunktion, Mathematische Zeitschrift 41 (1936), 405-414, as in Linnik and Ostrovskii, Decomposition of Random Variables and Vectors, AMS, 1977.

statement: Let a plane $\pi$ that misses the apex cut a right circular cone in a [conic section](c:conic-section) that is a closed curve $E$. The two spheres inside the cone that are tangent to the cone and to $\pi$ touch $\pi$ at points $F_1$ and $F_2$. Then $E$ is an ellipse with [foci](c:focal-point) $F_1$ and $F_2$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a right circular cone with apex $V$, and the plane $\pi$ does not contain $V$.
The plane $\pi$ meets every generator of one nappe of $K$, so $E = \pi \cap K$ is a closed curve.
$S_1$ and $S_2$ are spheres inside that nappe, [tangent](c:tangent-sphere) to $K$ and to $\pi$, on opposite sides of $\pi$, and $S_i$ touches $\pi$ at $F_i$.

conclusion: For every $P \in E$, $PF_1 + PF_2 = 2a$, where $2a$ is the distance along a generator between the two circles of tangency, and $E$ is the whole ellipse $\{P \in \pi : PF_1 + PF_2 = 2a\}$.

proofs.name: Equal tangent segments
proofs.slogan: Join each point of the section to the two circles of tangency, equate tangent segments from the point, and add them to get a constant sum.
proofs.scope: The ellipse case. The hyperbola case (spheres in the two nappes, constant $|PF_1 - PF_2|$) and the parabola case (one sphere, focus and directrix) are the other members of the family.

roles.why: Rotational symmetry about the axis makes the distance between the two circles the same on every generator, and $V \notin \pi$ makes $E$ an irreducible conic.
Each generator meets $\pi$ once, in a point $P$ of $E$, which fixes the position of $P$ on the generator.
The spheres give the circles of tangency and the equal tangent segments from $P$.

steps.slogan: Name the circles where $S_1$ and $S_2$ touch the cone, and the points where one generator meets them.
steps.detail: By symmetry about the axis, $S_i$ touches $K$ along a circle $C_i$ in a plane perpendicular to the axis. For $P \in E$, the generator $VP$ meets $C_i$ in one point $A_i$, where it touches $S_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that $P$ lies between $A_1$ and $A_2$ on the generator.
steps.detail: The spheres lie on opposite sides of $\pi$, and $A_i \notin \pi$ because $S_i$ meets $\pi$ only at $F_i$, which is off the cone. So $A_1$ and $A_2$ are on opposite sides of $\pi$. The generator meets $\pi$ only at $P$, so $P$ lies between $A_1$ and $A_2$ and $A_1A_2 = A_1P + PA_2$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two tangent segments from $P$ to each sphere.
steps.detail: The segment $PF_i$ lies in $\pi$, which touches $S_i$ at $F_i$, so $PF_i$ is tangent to $S_i$. The segment $PA_i$ lies on a generator that touches $S_i$ at $A_i$. Two tangent segments from one point to a [sphere](c:tangent-sphere) have equal length, so $PF_i = PA_i$.

steps.slogan: Add the equal segments to get $PF_1 + PF_2 = A_1A_2$.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $PF_1 + PF_2 = PA_1 + PA_2 = A_1A_2$. Rotational symmetry makes the distance along a generator between the parallel circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ the same for every generator; call it $2a$.

steps.slogan: Show that $E$ is the whole ellipse $\{P \in \pi : PF_1 + PF_2 = 2a\}$.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives $E \subseteq \mathcal{E} = \{P \in \pi : PF_1 + PF_2 = 2a\}$, and $2a > F_1F_2$ because $E$ is not a segment. Both $E$ and the ellipse $\mathcal{E}$ are irreducible [conic sections](c:conic-section), since $\pi$ misses $V$, and two irreducible conics with infinitely many common points coincide by Bézout. So $E = \mathcal{E}$ and $F_1, F_2$ are its [foci](c:focal-point).

concepts.c:tangent-sphere: The spheres touch the cone and the plane, giving equal tangent segments.
concepts.c:conic-section: The section is a conic, and a conic with infinitely many shared points is determined.
concepts.c:focal-point: The foci are the points where the spheres touch the plane.

source.note: The classical proof of G. P. Dandelin (1822) for the ellipse.

statement: Let $M$ be a [super-Cartan geometry](c:super-cartan-geometry) of bosonic dimension $d \ge 4$ whose structure group is the Lorentzian [spin group](c:spin-group), with [torsion](c:torsion-tensor) $T$ and curvature $R$. Then the components of $R$ are linear combinations of components of $\nabla T$ and products of torsion components, and the Bianchi identity of $R$ follows from that of $T$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [super-Cartan geometry](c:super-cartan-geometry) of bosonic dimension $d \ge 4$, with supervielbein $E^A$, Lorentz connection $\Omega$, torsion $T$ and curvature $R$.
The structure group is the Lorentzian [spin group](c:spin-group), so it acts on the vector frame $E^a$ and on the spinor frame $E^\alpha$.

conclusion: The curvature is a fixed linear function of $\nabla T$ and of products of torsion components, and the second Bianchi identity $\nabla R = 0$ holds as a consequence of the first.

proofs.name: Solving the first Bianchi identity
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the structure equations twice, solve the first Bianchi identity for the Lorentz curvature, and check that the second identity adds nothing.
proofs.scope: An outline: the algebra of the solution step (step 3) and the vanishing of the second identity rest on the cited paper. The bound $d \ge 4$ is needed, and the statement fails in bosonic dimension at most $3$.

roles.why: The supervielbein and connection define $T$ and $R$ and give the two Bianchi identities by $\nabla^2 = R$.
The spin group makes $R$ Lorentz-algebra valued, with a faithful spinor action, so the spinor part of the identity determines $R$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the structure equations twice to obtain both Bianchi identities.
steps.detail:
Write $T^A = 
abla E^A$ for the [super vielbein](c:super-vielbein) $E^A$ and $R = d\Omega + \Omega \wedge \Omega$. Then $
abla T^A = R^A{}_B \wedge E^B$ (the first identity) and $
abla R^A{}_B = 0$ (the second identity), because $
abla^2$ acts on tensors by the curvature.

steps.slogan: Read the first identity in the components of the supervielbein frame.
steps.detail: The identity $\nabla T^A = R^A{}_B \wedge E^B$ becomes algebraic equations that link components of $\nabla T$, products $TT$ and components of $R$. The components are sorted by the bosonic or fermionic type of their form indices.

steps.slogan: Use the spinor part of the identity to solve for the Lorentz curvature.
steps.detail: The Lorentz curvature acts on the spinor frame through the spin representation, so the identity for $T^\alpha$ contains $R^\alpha{}_\beta$, a linear image of $R^{ab}$, wedged with $E^\beta$. Since this action is faithful and $R^{ab}$ is antisymmetric, the equations determine every component of $R$ when $d \ge 4$.

steps.slogan: Collect the solved components into one linear expression in $\nabla T$ and $TT$.
steps.detail: Solving the linear system gives $R = L(\nabla T + T\,T)$, where $L$ is a fixed linear map built from invariant tensors of the Lorentz group. No further derivative of $T$ enters.

steps.slogan: Show that the second Bianchi identity follows from the first.
steps.detail:
Applying $
abla$ to the first identity gives $
abla R^A{}_B \wedge E^B = 0$, because $
abla^2 T^A = R^A{}_B \wedge T^B$. The cited paper shows that the algebra which solved for $R$ then forces $
abla R = 0$, so no new condition arises.

concepts.c:super-cartan-geometry: It supplies the supervielbein, connection, torsion and curvature of the theorem.
concepts.c:spin-group: The spin group makes the curvature Lorentz valued, with a faithful spinor action.
concepts.c:torsion-tensor: The torsion is the quantity that determines the curvature.
concepts.c:super-vielbein: The frame $E^A$ defines the torsion and the Bianchi identities.

source.ref: N. Dragon, Torsion and curvature in extended supergravity, Zeitschrift für Physik C 2 (1979), 29-32
source.note: Dragon expresses the curvature through the torsion and its covariant derivatives by the first Bianchi identity, and shows that the second identity then holds. The failure in bosonic dimension at most 3 (Dragon windows) is due to later work of Cederwall, Gran and Nilsson.

statement: Let $M$ be a [globally hyperbolic spacetime](c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime). Then $M$ has a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface) $S$, and $M$ is [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to $\mathbb{R} \times S$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a smooth, connected, time-oriented [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold).
$M$ is globally hyperbolic: it is strongly causal, and the causal diamonds $J^+(p) \cap J^-(q)$ are compact.

conclusion: The spacetime has a Cauchy surface $S$, a topological hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible timelike curve, and $M$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R} \times S$.

proofs.name: Geroch's volume time function
proofs.slogan: Build a continuous time function from volumes of causal pasts and futures, take a level set as the Cauchy surface, and flow along a timelike field.
proofs.scope: An outline of the proof of Geroch (1970), which carries out the continuity and surface claims of steps 2 to 4. Bernal and Sanchez later improved the splitting to a smooth one.

roles.why: The smooth structure gives a finite measure and a timelike vector field whose integral curves are timelike curves.
Compact diamonds and strong causality make the volume functions continuous and make timelike curves leave every diamond.

steps.slogan: Choose a finite measure $\mu$ on $M$ with a positive smooth density.
steps.detail: The manifold $M$ is second countable, so it carries a smooth positive function $\rho$ with $\int_M \rho\,dV = 1$. Then $\mu = \rho\,dV$ is a finite measure, and every nonempty open set has positive measure.

steps.slogan: Define $t(p) = \ln\big(\mu(J^-(p))/\mu(J^+(p))\big)$ and show that it is continuous and increasing along causal curves.
steps.detail: Global hyperbolicity makes $p \mapsto \mu(J^\pm(p))$ continuous, and both values are positive and finite. If $q \in J^+(p)$ and $q \ne p$, then $J^-(p) \subsetneq J^-(q)$ and $J^+(q) \subsetneq J^+(p)$, so $t(q) > t(p)$. Hence $t$ strictly increases along future causal curves.

steps.slogan: Show that $t$ takes every real value on each inextendible causal curve.
steps.detail: Along a future inextendible causal curve $\gamma$, the sets $J^+(\gamma(\tau))$ decrease and have empty intersection, because a common point would trap $\gamma$ in a compact diamond. So $\mu(J^+(\gamma(\tau))) \to 0$ while $\mu(J^-(\gamma(\tau)))$ increases, and $t \to +\infty$. The past direction gives $t \to -\infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that the level set $S = t^{-1}(0)$ is a Cauchy surface.
steps.detail: Each inextendible [timelike curve](c:timelike-curve) meets $S$ exactly once, since $t$ is continuous, strictly increasing along it and onto $\mathbb{R}$. A level set of a continuous function that increases strictly along causal curves is an achronal topological hypersurface. So $S$ is a [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface).

steps.slogan: Flow along a timelike vector field to identify $M$ with $\mathbb{R} \times S$.
steps.detail: Let $X$ be a smooth future-directed timelike vector field. Each maximal integral curve is an inextendible timelike curve, so it meets $S$ once and $t$ maps it onto $\mathbb{R}$. Sending $(s, q)$ to the point of the curve through $q \in S$ where $t = s$ gives a continuous bijection $\mathbb{R} \times S \to M$, hence a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) by invariance of domain.

concepts.c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime: Global hyperbolicity is the hypothesis that makes the volume time function work.
concepts.c:cauchy-surface: A level set of the time function is the Cauchy surface.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The flow gives a continuous bijection that is a homeomorphism.
concepts.c:lorentzian-manifold: The Lorentzian structure gives the causal sets and timelike curves.
concepts.c:timelike-curve: Inextendible timelike curves meet the level set exactly once.

source.ref: R. Geroch, Domain of dependence, Journal of Mathematical Physics 11 (1970), 437-449
source.note: Geroch introduces the volume functions and proves that global hyperbolicity is equivalent to the existence of a Cauchy surface; the splitting follows from the flow argument. A. N. Bernal and M. Sanchez, Commun. Math. Phys. 243 (2003), 461-470, give the smooth version.
